results.title: [2406.03248] Large Language Models as Evaluators for Recommendation Explanations

item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating recommendation relevance, explanation grounding, and user satisfaction. [ALERT (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.137/) evaluates explanations across 15 Amazon categories using purchase histories; its reported 70% concordance with expert judgments shows that automated assessment remains imperfect. [Large Language Models as Evaluators for Recommendation Explanations (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03248) compares LLM judgments with real-user feedback and third-party annotations, supporting direct validation against users rather than treating plausible explanations as ground truth. [Miscalibrated Conversational Priors (2024)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/on-overcoming-miscalibrated-conversational-priors-in-llm-based-chatbots/) documents incorrect assumptions under underspecified requests. [REGEN (2025)](https://research.google/blog/regen-empowering-personalized-recommendations-with-natural-language/) offers critique-based recommendation tasks, but its synthetic critiques and purchase reasons are not observed user intent.\n\nPractical synthesis for this task: annotate three independent dimensions—recent-interest alignment, possible redundancy, and item-identity clarity—with supported/contradicted/unknown states and evidence spans from histories, timestamps, titles, descriptions, or explicitly collected feedback. Recent-history similarity is an alignment proxy, not proof of current intent; descriptive similarity indicates possible redundancy, not ownership or rejection. Missing or ambiguous identifying attributes justify identity uncertainty. Compatibility, ownership, mood, purchase intent, and diversity/conformity preferences remain unknown unless explicitly supported. Validate this proposed rubric on the twenty training-user feedback cases using independent annotation and adjudication; report per-label counts, agreement, proxy precision/recall, and unknown coverage, with user-level uncertainty. Treat the small sample as exploratory calibration, retain unsupported cases as unknown, and keep these diagnostics separate from the fixed macro validation HR@10 used for model selection."}
